newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Roadblocks remain as Somalis await faction chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Roadblocks remain as Somalis await faction chiefs.

text.p: Roadblocks remained in place in the divided Somali capital Mogadishu and rival militia forces held their positions as the city awaited the return of faction leaders from talks in Kenya after announcing a peace agreement.
Somali sources said on Thursday faction members were waiting to hear details on how to implement the agreement which former colonial power Italy hailed as a breakthrough.

It was not known when the faction leaders -- Hussein Aideed, Ali Mahdi Mohamed and Ali Hassan Osman Atto -- would return to Somalia from the Kenyan capital. Aideed's faction was due to hold a news conference in Nairobi later on Thursday.
"We have heard everything, now we must be told by the leadership what we should exactly do," said Ali Abdul, a militiaman loyal to Hussein Aideed in south Mogadishu.

The agreement had not immediately changed anything on the ground in Mogadishu, which remained divided into the northern stronghold of Ali Mahdi and the southern region held by Aideed, with Atto in between.
"The roadblocks are still around and there haven't been any celebrations yet. People are still awaiting the return of the leaders. We will see how it goes," said one resident.
The agreement, one of many signed by Somali factions since the country disintegrated after the 1991 overthrow of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre, was announced late on Tuesday after a week of contacts.

A Kenyan statement said Somali leaders declared an end to hostilities, including media propaganda, with immediate effect, agreed to allow free movement of people in the capital and remove all roadblocks between their areas of control.
They also agreed to facilitate delivery of humanitarian aid to Somalis and pledged continued dialogue among themselves.

Officials said the three faction heads had met face-to-face three times. Somali sources said it was the first direct meeting between Ali Mahdi and Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine who took over from his father Mohamed Farah Aideed following his death in Mogadishu on August 1.
Aideed, like his father, was elected president of Somalia by supporters and heads a government recognised only by Libya and Sudan.
Italy, a former colonial power, said it welcomed the latest peace agreement and thanked Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi for bringing the Somalis together in his country.

"Italy followed the peace negotiations very closely; we visited the various delagations separately and at the venue for talks. We are concerned about Somalia and would like to see a return to peace and normalcy there," an embassy spokesman said.
Somali officials insisted the deal was reached without Moi.
